caption:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told staff on November 8 that he was unfaithful to his wife and apologized.
The New York Times reported he told Nvidia's board the relationship was with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive US intelligence officials believe worked for China.
Nvidia's independent directors, with outside lawyers, are now investigating. The board says it has no reason to believe secrets or national security were compromised, and Huang stays CEO.

Should Huang stay in charge while the probe runs?

paragraphs.text: Nvidia's board of directors opened an independent inquiry on Sunday, November 8, 2026, into chief executive Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a woman US officials believe is a Chinese intelligence asset. The announcement came the same day Huang told employees in a companywide memo that he had been unfaithful to his wife.

In the memo, Huang apologized to his family and to staff, wrote that his actions had hurt his wife and children, and said he took full responsibility. The memo did not name the woman or directly address the spying allegations, according to The San Francisco Standard. Huang also wrote that he is committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting American national security, and said he supports the board's review.

The New York Times first reported on October 29 that US intelligence officials had concluded that Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, worked for the Chinese government and had grown close to the Nvidia chief. She is not related to him. On November 6, the Financial Times reported that a US government memo described a romantic relationship between the two, The San Francisco Standard said.

According to the Times, as cited by Fox Business and The San Francisco Standard, Jensen Huang acknowledged to Nvidia's board on November 8 that the relationship was with Alice Huang. The Times also reported that she gathered information for Beijing, and that US officials initially did not believe the Nvidia chief knew of her alleged intelligence work. The Chinese government has called the allegations groundless speculation.

In an interview with Bloomberg in October, Huang had described his interactions with Alice Huang as related to Megaspeed's business and not unusual, The San Francisco Standard reported. US officials scrutinized Megaspeed in 2024 over suspicions that it helped Chinese companies get around American chip export rules. Nvidia says there is no evidence its products are smuggled to China.

A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside legal counsel, will oversee the inquiry, according to the board's statement. It will look at whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort and whether company secrets or US national security interests were compromised. The board said it currently has no reason to believe that either was compromised and that it will examine all available information.

The directors said US national and economic security come before the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders, Fox Business reported. The board also said it has confidence in Huang and his leadership team. Huang, 63, remains chief executive, and an Nvidia spokesperson said the news would not slow the company.

Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, the Republican chairs of the House Foreign Affairs, China select and Intelligence committees, asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing on November 18 about his contacts with Alice Huang and Nvidia's protections against foreign espionage. Senator Chris Coons, a Delaware Democrat, said Congress would investigate, according to The San Francisco Standard.

The timing adds to the scrutiny. Nvidia is scheduled to report third quarter earnings on November 17, one day before the requested briefing. Huang has also lobbied the Trump administration to ease limits on Nvidia chip sales to China, Fox Business noted.

The board's early statement does two things at once: it backs Huang as chief executive and it commits to an outside review of a national security question. That balance may be hard to hold if Congress or the inquiry produces new details, because Nvidia's business with China already sits at the center of US export policy.
Watch the November 17 earnings call and the November 18 House briefing request for the first signs of what the inquiry has found and whether Huang agrees to appear.
